questions.stem: A 63 year old man is brought by his wife, who says that for 5 years he has shouted and kicked out while dreaming. He lost his sense of smell some years ago. Over 8 months his handwriting has become small and he is slow doing up buttons. He has reduced facial expression and reduced right arm swing. Memory is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: REM sleep behaviour disorder and loss of smell are early features that can precede motor signs; asymmetric bradykinesia and hypomimia confirm Parkinson's disease.

clues: shouted and kicked out while dreaming
steps.x: Prodromal REM sleep behaviour disorder and anosmia, then asymmetric bradykinesia.

elim: Cognitive decline and visual hallucinations come early; his memory is normal.
A symmetrical action tremor without bradykinesia or a sleep disorder.
Severe early autonomic failure, which he does not have.
Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline.

steps.x: E: Parkinson's disease. RBD + anosmia + asymmetric bradykinesia = Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has a 1 year history of a resting tremor of her left hand and slowness when walking. A movement disorder specialist diagnoses Parkinson's disease. When asked about her past health, she recalls a symptom that started several years before the tremor.
questions.q: Which symptom is most likely to have come before her motor symptoms?
questions.e: Olfactory loss can precede the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease by years, as can REM sleep behaviour disorder.

clues: started several years before the tremor
steps.x: Which non-motor feature is a known early indicator of PD?

elim: A side effect of levodopa, or Huntington's disease.
A complication of long-term levodopa, not a prodrome.
Bell's palsy or stroke.
Usually late, or from medication; early hallucinations suggest Lewy body dementia.

steps.x: B: Loss of sense of smell. Anosmia is an early (prodromal) indicator of PD.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has noticed shaking of his right hand for 6 months. His daughter says it is most obvious when he is sitting watching television with his hands in his lap. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines. His GP examines the tremor carefully.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: 4 Hz tremor that lessens when he reaches for a cup
Bilateral flapping tremor with outstretched hands
Fine 10 Hz tremor of both outstretched hands
Symmetrical action tremor that improves with alcohol
Tremor that worsens as his finger approaches a target
questions.e: The tremor of Parkinson's disease is a resting, pill-rolling, asymmetric 3 to 5 Hz tremor that improves with voluntary movement.

steps.x: A one-sided tremor most obvious at rest.

elim: Asterixis of liver failure or CO2 retention.
A physiological or thyrotoxic tremor.
Typical of essential tremor.
An intention tremor from cerebellar disease.

steps.x: A: 4 Hz tremor that lessens when he reaches for a cup. PD tremor: rest, 3 to 5 Hz, asymmetric, better with movement.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 9 month history of slowness and a tremor of her left hand at rest. Her left arm is stiff on passive movement. Her right side is normal. She has never taken antipsychotics or antiemetics. Her BP is 136/80 mmHg lying and 132/78 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is typically asymmetrical; symmetrical tremor suggests essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.

clues: tremor of her left hand at rest
steps.x: One-sided rest tremor with rigidity, no drugs and no postural drop.

elim: Usually symmetrical and she has not taken any dopamine antagonists.
A symmetrical postural or action tremor without rigidity or bradykinesia.
Has early autonomic failure; her BP does not fall on standing.
Symmetrical, with early falls and a vertical gaze palsy.

steps.x: C: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Asymmetric parkinsonism without autonomic failure or drugs = idiopathic PD.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has had Parkinson's disease for 9 years. His symptoms started with a tremor of his right hand and responded very well to co-careldopa. Only in the last year has he developed constipation and mild dizziness on standing. His tremor is still more marked on the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation of his autonomic symptoms?
o: Late autonomic involvement in Parkinson's disease
questions.e: In idiopathic PD autonomic dysfunction occurs later; severe early autonomic failure with atremulous parkinsonism suggests MSA.

steps.x: Tremor-dominant, asymmetric, levodopa-responsive disease with autonomic features appearing only after many years.

elim: Does not cause autonomic symptoms or respond to levodopa.
Causes severe autonomic failure early, with atremulous parkinsonism and a poor levodopa response.
Causes early falls and a gaze palsy, with a poor levodopa response.
Affects the legs symmetrically with a poor levodopa response.

steps.x: B: Late autonomic involvement in Parkinson's disease. Autonomic dysfunction late = PD; early and severe = MSA.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had a 1 year history of slowness and stiffness of his left arm. His wife says he looks miserable even when he is enjoying himself and rarely blinks. His speech is quiet. His mood screening questionnaire is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his face?
o: Bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness
Left lower facial droop sparing the forehead
Ptosis worse at the end of the day
questions.e: Hypomimia (reduced facial expression) with reduced blinking is part of the bradykinesia of Parkinson's disease.

clues: slowness and stiffness of his left arm
looks miserable even when he is enjoying himself
steps.x: A mask-like face with a normal mood, alongside asymmetric bradykinesia.

elim: Seen in Guillain-Barré syndrome or sarcoidosis.
An upper motor neurone lesion such as stroke.
Myasthenia gravis.
Progressive supranuclear palsy.

steps.x: D: Reduced facial expression. Hypomimia is a PD sign, not depression.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has had Parkinson's disease for 6 years and has fallen three times this year. Standing behind her, the doctor gives a sharp pull backwards on her shoulders. She walks with a stooped posture and small steps that seem to speed up as she goes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on this test?
o: Several steps backwards without recovering balance
Swaying only when the eyes are closed
questions.e: Postural instability in Parkinson's disease shows as retropulsion on the pull test, with a stooped, shuffling, festinating gait and falls.

steps.x: Falls, stooped posture and festination: postural instability.

elim: A cerebellar sign.
A peripheral neuropathy or common peroneal nerve palsy.
A positive Romberg test from sensory ataxia.
Proximal myopathy or hip disease.

steps.x: C: Several steps backwards without recovering balance. PD postural instability: retropulsion on the pull test.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has had Parkinson's disease for 11 years and takes co-careldopa five times a day. Several times a day she suddenly freezes and cannot move for 20 to 30 minutes, then just as suddenly can move freely again. These episodes happen at random, unrelated to when she takes her tablets.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Unpredictable switching between mobility and immobility unrelated to dose timing is the on-off phenomenon, a motor fluctuation of long-term levodopa.

clues: at random, unrelated to when she takes her tablets
steps.x: Sudden, random motor fluctuations after many years of levodopa.

elim: Would cause abnormal movements or altered awareness, not sudden immobility in someone with long-standing PD.
Fever, rigidity and autonomic instability after a dopamine antagonist.
Involuntary writhing movements about an hour after each dose.
A predictable return of symptoms just before the next dose.

steps.x: C: On-off phenomenon. Random on-off switching = on-off phenomenon; predictable end-of-dose = wearing-off.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has had Parkinson's disease for 12 years. Over 18 months his wife has noticed he is slower to think, gets lost in conversations and struggles to plan simple tasks. There has been no sudden change, he has no fever and his urine dipstick is negative. His MMSE is 21/30.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dementia is a late complication of Parkinson's disease, alongside falls, dyskinesia and motor fluctuations.

steps.x: Gradual cognitive decline many years into PD.

elim: Usually starts with memory loss, not in someone with a long motor illness.
An acute, fluctuating change, often with an infection; this is gradual.
Dementia comes before or within a year of parkinsonism, not 10 years later.
Gait apraxia and urinary incontinence with ventricular enlargement.

steps.x: E: Parkinson's disease dementia. Dementia long after motor onset = PD dementia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with Parkinson's disease controlled on co-careldopa sees his GP with dizziness and vomiting from labyrinthitis and is given a new medicine. A week later he is much slower, stiffer and is shuffling. Other medicines: amlodipine, simvastatin, senna and paracetamol.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused the deterioration?
questions.e: Dopamine antagonists such as prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, droperidol and haloperidol worsen Parkinson's disease; prochlorperazine is often given for vertigo.

steps.x: Worse parkinsonism after a new medicine for vertigo and vomiting.

elim: Long-standing, and does not block dopamine receptors.
Does not affect dopamine.
A laxative with no effect on parkinsonism.
Long-standing; does not worsen parkinsonism.

steps.x: C: Prochlorperazine. Prochlorperazine is a dopamine antagonist: avoid in PD.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease a year ago and started ropinirole for mild symptoms. His wife has found he has spent £14,000 on online gambling over 3 months and has started compulsively buying gadgets. He had no previous history of gambling. His other medicine is amlodipine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his behaviour?
questions.e: Dopamine agonists carry the highest risk of impulse control disorders such as gambling and compulsive shopping, and are contraindicated if one already exists.

steps.x: New compulsive gambling after starting a dopamine agonist.

elim: Does not cause compulsive behaviour.
No other features of mania and no previous history.
Would come with personality change and cognitive decline, not starting with a new drug.
A late complication, and gambling is not its typical feature.

steps.x: E: Ropinirole. Dopamine agonists: highest risk of impulse control disorders.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with Parkinson's disease started co-careldopa 2 weeks ago. She now feels dizzy when she stands up and nearly fainted in the kitchen. Her BP is 138/82 mmHg lying and 108/66 mmHg after 3 minutes standing. She is drinking well and has no diarrhoea.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her dizziness?
questions.e: Postural hypotension is a common side effect of levodopa, along with abnormal dreams, dyskinesias, dystonia and early morning hypokinesia.

steps.x: A postural BP drop starting soon after levodopa.

elim: She is drinking well with no fluid losses.
Would cause early severe autonomic failure, not a drop timed to a new drug.
Would cause palpitations and does not explain a reproducible postural drop.
Has a trigger and prodrome, and BP does not drop on every standing.

steps.x: A: Co-careldopa. Levodopa causes postural hypotension.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 1 year history of a resting tremor of his right hand, slowness and stiffness. A movement disorder specialist diagnoses idiopathic Parkinson's disease and explains that the symptoms come from dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the primary neuronal loss?
questions.e: Parkinson's disease is dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

clues: dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia
steps.x: Where do the dopaminergic neurons that supply the striatum live?

elim: Atrophies in Huntington's disease.
Damaged by alcohol, causing gait ataxia.
Damaged in internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
A lesion causes hemiballismus.

steps.x: D: Substantia nigra. PD: loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 7 month history of a resting tremor of her right hand, slowness and stiffness of the right arm. She has no autonomic symptoms or cognitive problems. A movement disorder specialist sees her in clinic and asks the medical student how Parkinson's disease is usually diagnosed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
questions.e: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis, made by a movement disorder specialist after urgent neurology referral.

clues: resting tremor of her right hand
how Parkinson's disease is usually diagnosed
steps.x: Typical asymmetric parkinsonism with no red flags.

elim: Normal in Parkinson's disease.
Only used if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Excludes other causes but does not diagnose PD.
Screens for Wilson's disease in young patients.

steps.x: A: Clinical assessment by the specialist. PD is a clinical diagnosis by a specialist; DaTSCAN only if uncertain.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man sees his GP with a 4 month history of a resting tremor of his left hand and slow, small handwriting. On examination he has left-sided cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia. He asks whether he can start some tablets today.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Arrange a DaTSCAN from primary care
Refer urgently to neurology before starting treatment
questions.e: Suspected Parkinson's disease should be referred urgently, untreated, to a specialist who makes the clinical diagnosis and starts treatment.

clues: resting tremor of his left hand
steps.x: Classic suspected PD in primary care.

elim: Not a GP test, and only used if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Suspected PD needs prompt specialist assessment.
Treatment should be started by a specialist after diagnosis.
Treatment should be started by a specialist after diagnosis.

steps.x: B: Refer urgently to neurology before starting treatment. Suspected PD: refer urgently, do not treat first.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 3 years. She now has slowness and a tremor of both hands. Her psychiatrist feels she cannot stop the risperidone safely. The neurologist wants to know whether she has drug-induced parkinsonism or underlying Parkinson's disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: DaTSCAN shows reduced dopamine transporter activity in Parkinson's disease and is normal in drug-induced parkinsonism; it is used when the diagnosis is uncertain.

clues: drug-induced parkinsonism or underlying Parkinson's disease
steps.x: Uncertain diagnosis because of a dopamine antagonist.

elim: Does not show dopaminergic loss.
Used for seizures.
Has no role in PD.
Is raised by risperidone and does not help.

steps.x: B: DaTSCAN. Uncertain parkinsonism: DaTSCAN.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has Parkinson's disease diagnosed by a neurologist a year ago. She now cannot dress herself or cook without help because of slowness and stiffness, and she has fallen once. She has no impulse control problems. The neurologist plans to start levodopa.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate preparation?
questions.e: Levodopa is given with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa as co-careldopa, or benserazide as co-beneldopa) for significant functional impairment.

clues: cannot dress herself or cook without help
steps.x: Significant impairment: levodopa, always with a decarboxylase inhibitor.

elim: Used mainly for dyskinesia, not as first-line treatment.
A COMT inhibitor that only works alongside levodopa.
A dopamine antagonist that worsens PD.
Without a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, most is broken down outside the brain and side effects are worse.

steps.x: B: Co-beneldopa. Levodopa + benserazide = co-beneldopa.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man is diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a neurologist. He has a mild tremor of his right hand that does not interfere with work. He was treated for a gambling addiction 5 years ago. He would like a medicine to help his symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: For mild symptoms, dopamine agonists or MAO-B inhibitors are used; agonists carry the highest impulse control risk and are contraindicated here, so an MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline) is best.

steps.x: Mild PD, but dopamine agonists are ruled out by a past impulse control disorder.

elim: A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
A dopamine antagonist antiemetic; worsens PD.
A dopamine agonist, contraindicated with an existing impulse control disorder.
A dopamine agonist, contraindicated with an existing impulse control disorder.

steps.x: D: Rasagiline. Mild PD with ICD history: MAO-B inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has Parkinson's disease newly diagnosed by a neurologist. Her symptoms are mild: a slight tremor and slowness of her left hand that do not affect her job as a teacher. She has no history of impulse control or psychiatric problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Mild symptoms can be treated with a dopamine agonist such as ropinirole (or an MAO-B inhibitor), provided there is no existing impulse control disorder.

steps.x: Mild PD without impulse control problems.

elim: An antiemetic, not a treatment for PD itself.
A COMT inhibitor added to levodopa for motor fluctuations; useless alone.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
Used for PD psychosis, not motor symptoms.

steps.x: E: Ropinirole. Mild PD: dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had Parkinson's disease for 5 years and takes co-careldopa three times a day. His tremor and stiffness come back about an hour before each dose is due and settle soon after he takes it. He has no dyskinesias.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial step in management?
o: Increase the frequency of co-careldopa doses
questions.e: Wearing-off (predictable end-of-dose return of symptoms) is managed first by increasing levodopa frequency.

clues: come back about an hour before each dose is due
settle soon after he takes it
steps.x: Predictable end-of-dose return of symptoms: wearing-off.

elim: A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
Would cause severe deterioration.
An antiemetic, not a PD treatment.

steps.x: C: Increase the frequency of co-careldopa doses. Wearing-off: give levodopa more often.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had Parkinson's disease for 8 years. Despite co-careldopa five times a day, her mobility now swings between good and poor periods through the day. Her neurologist wants to add a drug that reduces the peripheral breakdown of levodopa.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to add?
questions.e: Motor fluctuations are managed by adding an MAO-B inhibitor, a COMT inhibitor such as entacapone, or a dopamine agonist.

clues: swings between good and poor periods
reduces the peripheral breakdown of levodopa
steps.x: Motor fluctuations on levodopa: add an adjunct that stops it being broken down.

elim: An antiemetic; does not affect levodopa breakdown.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
Treats PD psychosis, not motor fluctuations.

steps.x: B: Entacapone. Motor fluctuations: add a COMT inhibitor (entacapone).

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with Parkinson's disease on co-careldopa is admitted with small bowel obstruction. She is vomiting, has a nasogastric tube on free drainage and is nil by mouth while awaiting surgery. The nurse asks what to do about her Parkinson's medicine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop all Parkinson's medicines until she is eating
questions.e: If oral levodopa cannot be taken, a transdermal dopamine agonist patch (rotigotine) is used as rescue to prevent acute dystonia and crisis.

clues: what to do about her Parkinson's medicine
steps.x: PD medicines are time-critical, but she cannot absorb anything orally.

elim: A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
She is vomiting with an obstructed gut and cannot absorb tablets.
Medicines are time-critical; stopping them risks crisis.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.

steps.x: E: Transdermal dopamine agonist patch. Nil by mouth in PD: transdermal dopamine agonist patch.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted for an elective hip replacement tomorrow. He takes co-careldopa at 7am, 11am, 3pm and 7pm. A junior nurse suggests giving his tablets with the morning drug round at 10am to make things easier.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate instruction about his Parkinson's medicine?
o: Give each dose at his usual times
Halve the doses while in hospital
questions.e: Parkinson's medicines are time-critical and must never be stopped or delayed on admission, including around surgery.

clues: with the morning drug round at 10am
steps.x: Moving doses to fit the drug round delays them.

elim: Changes the timing; PD medicines are time-critical.
Risks a Parkinsonian crisis.
Never stop PD medicines on admission.
A dopamine antagonist that worsens PD.

steps.x: B: Give each dose at his usual times. PD medicines are time-critical: give on time, every time.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with Parkinson's disease has had three falls and increasing confusion over 2 months. Her medicines are co-careldopa, amitriptyline, oxybutynin, zopiclone, ropinirole and amlodipine, prescribed by different doctors. She has no fever and her urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Review her medicines for interactions and side effects
questions.e: Frequent medication reviews to check for interactions and polypharmacy are part of long-term PD care; anticholinergics and sedatives here can cause falls and confusion.

steps.x: Polypharmacy with anticholinergics and sedatives in an older PD patient.

elim: A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
Dopamine agonists can worsen confusion.
PD drugs are time-critical; stopping them causes crisis.

steps.x: D: Review her medicines for interactions and side effects. PD long term: regular medication reviews.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with Parkinson's disease on optimised co-careldopa has fallen twice at home and struggles to get dressed and in and out of the bath. He has no dizziness on standing, his BP does not fall on standing and his medicines were reviewed last month.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
questions.e: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are part of long-term PD management, helping falls, gait and daily activities.

clues: BP does not fall on standing
steps.x: Falls and functional problems despite optimised medicines.

elim: A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
The diagnosis is already established.
Do not address the cause of his falls or dressing problems.
Would make mobility worse.

steps.x: D: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy. PD long term: physio and OT for falls and function.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with Parkinson's disease is in recovery after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy and feels very sick. The anaesthetist lists several antiemetics that are available on the ward.
questions.q: Which antiemetic should be avoided?
questions.e: Droperidol, like metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol, is a central dopamine antagonist that worsens PD; domperidone is the antiemetic of choice.

steps.x: Which antiemetic blocks dopamine in the brain?

elim: An antihistamine antiemetic that does not block dopamine receptors.
A steroid antiemetic, safe in PD.
The antiemetic of choice in PD; it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
A 5-HT3 antagonist that does not worsen parkinsonism.

steps.x: D: Droperidol. Avoid central dopamine antagonists (droperidol) in PD.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with Parkinson's disease has delirium from a urinary tract infection. He is shouting, trying to hit staff and pulling at his cannula. De-escalation has failed and he is putting himself and others at risk. He is on antibiotics and his usual co-careldopa.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate rapid tranquillisation?
questions.e: In PD, rapid tranquillisation uses oral or IM lorazepam; haloperidol is contraindicated.

steps.x: Rapid tranquillisation is needed, but dopamine blockers are out.

elim: A typical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine.
Contraindicated in PD; it blocks dopamine and worsens parkinsonism.
A dopamine antagonist; worsens PD.
An antipsychotic with strong dopamine blockade.

steps.x: C: Lorazepam. PD rapid tranquillisation: lorazepam, never haloperidol.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with Parkinson's disease was admitted 2 days ago with a fractured wrist. Her drug chart shows that her co-careldopa has not been given since admission. Today she is rigid, cannot get out of bed or swallow well, and her temperature is 37.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Wait for the neurology ward round
questions.e: Sudden immobility after missed doses suggests a Parkinsonian crisis from medication failure; PD medicines are time-critical and must be restarted at once (by patch if she cannot swallow).

clues: has not been given since admission
rigid, cannot get out of bed
steps.x: Sudden severe worsening after missed levodopa.

elim: A dopamine antagonist that would worsen the crisis.
A dopamine antagonist that would worsen the crisis.
Delays treating the obvious cause.
This is an emergency; delay worsens it.

steps.x: D: Restart her Parkinson's medicine urgently. Parkinsonian crisis from missed doses: restart medication urgently.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with Parkinson's disease asks why loss of dopamine makes his movements slow and stiff. His neurologist explains how the basal ganglia normally balance two pathways that control movement.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bradykinesia?
o: Loss of upper motor neurones in the motor cortex
Overactivity of the direct pathway relative to the indirect pathway
Overactivity of the indirect pathway relative to the direct pathway
questions.e: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine disturbs the balance between the direct (facilitating) and indirect (inhibiting) pathways, so inhibition wins, causing bradykinesia and rigidity.

clues: loss of dopamine makes his movements slow and stiff
steps.x: Dopamine normally helps the 'go' pathway and suppresses the 'stop' pathway.

elim: PD is dopamine deficiency.
Causes ataxia, not bradykinesia.
Causes spastic weakness.
This would increase movement, not slow it.

steps.x: E: Overactivity of the indirect pathway relative to the direct pathway. PD: inhibitory indirect pathway dominates.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with a 9 year history of Parkinson's disease dies of a stroke. At post-mortem, the substantia nigra is pale. Microscopy of the remaining pigmented neurons shows round, eosinophilic structures inside the cytoplasm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely identity of these structures?
questions.e: The pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease is Lewy bodies, intracellular alpha-synuclein aggregates in surviving neurons.

clues: round, eosinophilic structures inside the cytoplasm
steps.x: Pale nigra with intracytoplasmic inclusions in PD.

elim: Actin inclusions seen in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
Inclusions of rabies infection.
Tau aggregates of Alzheimer's disease and PSP.
Tau inclusions of frontotemporal dementia.

steps.x: B: Lewy bodies. PD hallmark: Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein).

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has a 1 year history of a resting tremor and stiffness of his right arm only. A student asks the neurologist why the disease affects only one side when the brain has dopaminergic neurons on both sides.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for the asymmetry?
o: Dopamine antagonists act on one side
Neuronal loss is asymmetrical in early disease
Only the dominant hemisphere makes dopamine
Peripheral nerves on that side are damaged
There is a stroke in the left internal capsule
questions.e: Early PD is asymmetric because neuronal loss is asymmetric; this helps distinguish it from MSA and drug-induced parkinsonism.

steps.x: Why is idiopathic PD one-sided at the start?

elim: Drug effects are symmetrical, and he takes none.
Both substantia nigra make dopamine.
PD is a central disease.
This would cause weakness, not rest tremor.

steps.x: B: Neuronal loss is asymmetrical in early disease. Asymmetry reflects asymmetrical early neuronal loss.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with Parkinson's disease is given haloperidol in the emergency department for agitation. The next morning she is so rigid that she cannot sit up. Her temperature is 37.0°C and creatine kinase is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her deterioration?
o: Blockade of postsynaptic dopamine receptors in the striatum
questions.e: Dopamine antagonists block postsynaptic dopamine receptors in an already dopamine-depleted striatum, worsening parkinsonism.

clues: so rigid that she cannot sit up
steps.x: Severe rigidity after an antipsychotic, without fever or raised CK.

elim: Increases acetylcholine; not haloperidol's action.
Would increase dopamine and improve parkinsonism.
Would increase dopamine; this is how rasagiline helps.
This is how dopamine agonists improve PD.

steps.x: A: Blockade of postsynaptic dopamine receptors in the striatum. Dopamine antagonists block receptors in a depleted striatum.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had Parkinson's disease for 10 years. His motor fluctuations began after 6 years of oral co-careldopa three times a day. His neurologist explains that continuous delivery devices aim to smooth out the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his motor fluctuations?
o: Increased peripheral breakdown of levodopa over time
questions.e: Long-term oral levodopa gives pulsatile, non-physiological stimulation of dopamine receptors, causing motor fluctuations.

steps.x: Intermittent tablets give peaks and troughs; continuous delivery smooths them.

elim: These do not occur.
A separate condition that does not cause fluctuations.
Not the mechanism of fluctuations.
Nigral neurons do not regrow.

steps.x: D: Pulsatile stimulation of dopamine receptors. Motor fluctuations come from pulsatile receptor stimulation.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with Parkinson's disease has nausea from chemotherapy. Her oncologist prescribes domperidone rather than metoclopramide, even though both are dopamine antagonists.
questions.q: Which best explains why domperidone does not worsen her Parkinson's disease?
o: It does not cross the blood-brain barrier
questions.e: Domperidone blocks dopamine receptors peripherally but does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it does not worsen parkinsonism; it is the antiemetic of choice.

steps.x: Two dopamine antagonists; only one reaches the striatum.

elim: It does not.
It is a dopamine antagonist.
That is ondansetron.
That would make PD worse, not better.

steps.x: A: It does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Domperidone stays outside the brain.
